items.readable_text:
Content:
The slope of a line, denoted [MATH: m,] measures how steep the line is. It is given by the following formula:

Content:
[MATH: m = \dfrac{\color{red}{\textrm{rise}}}{\color{blue}{\textrm{run}}}]

Content:
Let's calculate the slope of the line that passes through the points [MATH: (1, 3)] and [MATH: (3, 7)], as shown below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/62cb84700681b5ec37254f7785fd66bd]

Content:
Moving from [MATH: (1, 3)] to [MATH: (3, 7)], the line rises vertically by [MATH: \color{red}4] units while running [MATH: \color{blue}2] units horizontally. Therefore, the slope of this line is

Content:
[MATH: m = \dfrac{\color{red}{\textrm{rise}}}{\color{blue}{\textrm{run}}} = \dfrac{\color{red}{4}}{\color{blue}{2}} = 2.]

Content:
The slope [MATH: m = 2] is a unit rate. It tells us the line rises vertically by [MATH: 2] units per unit of horizontal change.

Content:
Note the following:

Content:
- If a line moves upward as we move from left to right ([MATH: \nearrow]), its slope is positive because the line rises by a positive amount.
- If a line moves downward as we move from left to right ([MATH: \searrow]), its slope is negative because the line falls (meaning it rises by a negative amount).

Content:
Suppose that [MATH: (x_1, y_1)] and [MATH: (x_2, y_2)] are two points on a straight line, as shown below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/ddbc40bad24322b8089defab1cd8e284]

Content:
The "rise" of the line is [MATH: \color{red}y_2 - y_1,] and the "run" of the line is [MATH: \color{blue}x_2-x_1]. Therefore, we compute the slope [MATH: m] of the line as follows:

Content:
[MATH: m = \dfrac {y_2 - y_1} {x_2 - x_1}]

Content:
For vertical lines, the slope is undefined. This is because [MATH: x_2 - x_1 = 0,] which leads to division by zero in the above formula.

Content:
Note: We can pick any point on the line as our [MATH: (x_1,y_1)] and any other point on the line as [MATH: (x_2,y_2).] We will get the same answer for the slope no matter which pair of points we pick.

items.title: Calculating the Slope Given Two Points

sections.normalized_html: Calculate the slope of the line that passes through the points [MATH: (1, 5)] and [MATH: (4, 2).]
sections.readable_text: Calculate the slope of the line that passes through the points [MATH: (1, 5)] and [MATH: (4, 2).]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
We let [MATH: (x_1,y_1) = (1,5)] and [MATH: (x_2,y_2) = (4,2),] and compute the slope using the formula:

[MATH: \eqalign{ m &= \dfrac {y_2 - y_1} {x_2 - x_1} \ &= \dfrac {2 - 5} {4 - 1} \ &= \dfrac {-3}{3} \ &= -1 }]

Thus, the slope is [MATH: m=-1.]

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
The slope of a line, denoted [MATH: m,] measures how steep the line is. It is given by the following formula:

Content:
[MATH: m = \dfrac{\color{red}{\textrm{rise}}}{\color{blue}{\textrm{run}}}]

Content:
Let's calculate the slope of the line that passes through the points [MATH: (1, 3)] and [MATH: (3, 7)], as shown below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/62cb84700681b5ec37254f7785fd66bd]

Content:
Moving from [MATH: (1, 3)] to [MATH: (3, 7)], the line rises vertically by [MATH: \color{red}4] units while running [MATH: \color{blue}2] units horizontally. Therefore, the slope of this line is

Content:
[MATH: m = \dfrac{\color{red}{\textrm{rise}}}{\color{blue}{\textrm{run}}} = \dfrac{\color{red}{4}}{\color{blue}{2}} = 2.]

Content:
The slope [MATH: m = 2] is a unit rate. It tells us the line rises vertically by [MATH: 2] units per unit of horizontal change.

Content:
Note the following:

Content:
- If a line moves upward as we move from left to right ([MATH: \nearrow]), its slope is positive because the line rises by a positive amount.
- If a line moves downward as we move from left to right ([MATH: \searrow]), its slope is negative because the line falls (meaning it rises by a negative amount).

---

Item 2 — Tutorial: The General Formula for Slope

Content:
Suppose that [MATH: (x_1, y_1)] and [MATH: (x_2, y_2)] are two points on a straight line, as shown below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/ddbc40bad24322b8089defab1cd8e284]

Content:
The "rise" of the line is [MATH: \color{red}y_2 - y_1,] and the "run" of the line is [MATH: \color{blue}x_2-x_1]. Therefore, we compute the slope [MATH: m] of the line as follows:

Content:
[MATH: m = \dfrac {y_2 - y_1} {x_2 - x_1}]

Content:
For vertical lines, the slope is undefined. This is because [MATH: x_2 - x_1 = 0,] which leads to division by zero in the above formula.

Content:
Note: We can pick any point on the line as our [MATH: (x_1,y_1)] and any other point on the line as [MATH: (x_2,y_2).] We will get the same answer for the slope no matter which pair of points we pick.

---

Item 3 — Example: Calculating the Slope Given Two Points

Example Prompt:
Calculate the slope of the line that passes through the points [MATH: (1, 5)] and [MATH: (4, 2).]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
We let [MATH: (x_1,y_1) = (1,5)] and [MATH: (x_2,y_2) = (4,2),] and compute the slope using the formula:

[MATH: \eqalign{
m &= \dfrac {y_2 - y_1} {x_2 - x_1} \
&= \dfrac {2 - 5} {4 - 1} \
&= \dfrac {-3}{3} \
&= -1
}]

Thus, the slope is [MATH: m=-1.]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Remember that slope is the amount the line rises vertically per unit that it runs horizontally.

Since the graph decreases ([MATH: \searrow]) as we go from left to right, the line rises by a negative amount.

Therefore, the slope of the line is negative.
